SUE Design Manager User Guide

Appendix B

EDIF And SUE File Conversion

This appendix provides information about the EDIF2SUE and SUE2EDIF file converters. These tools can be used to convert schematics between SUE and other schematic editors.

edif2sue is a tool for translating an EDIF design file into a set of SUE cell files. edif2sue requires a special license to execute.

sue2edif is a plug-in addition to SUE for writing an EDIF design file based on the current design loaded in SUE. sue2edif requires a special license to execute.

EDIF To SUE Translator: "edif2sue"

Usage

edif2sue is a tool for translating an EDIF design file into a set of SUE cell files. This tool can be used to convert schematics generated with another schematic editor into SUE format. edif2sue requires a special license to execute.

A usage message is available by invoking edif2sue without parameters.

The most basic usage is: 

              edif2sue ediffile.edf

The above example (if ediffile.edf is a valid EDIF file) will create a set of files in the local subdirectory "sue", which should exist already.

The translation process consists of two parts, which are described below.

  1. Reading-in and parsing the EDIF file.

  2. Extracting and writing-out SUE files.

A tool to write EDIF files from SUE is available as a plug-in option to SUE; see sue2edif documentation in the next section.

Options

Options are specified in an e2s_rc file. The default file is 

      $MMI_TOOLS/edif2sue/e2s_rc.


An explicit path can be specified using the -config_file <path> command line option.

  • Any number of paths can be specified.
    •

  • Files will be read in the order specified.
    •

  • Calling edif2sue with no arguments will cause a usage message to be printed.
    •

  • Within the e2s_rc file, options are specified one per line.

  • The fields of the line are read using the scanf. See the man page for details.
    •

The first field is the option keyword, as specified below; following fields are parameters of the option, if required.

cellname_prefix: A complete design can be expected to contain low-level components such as transistors or simple gates whose name may collide with similar but probably not identical components in the local library. That will create an impossible situation if the intent is to edit the files. Therefore, the user should specify a prefix that will be applied to all the cell names extracted from the EDIF file (and consequently on the generated SUE files).

So for example: 

      cellname_prefix fred_

With the above option, a cell named "inverter" would be renamed to fred_inverter, and its definition would appear in a file called fred_inverter.sue.

outdir: Gives a relative or absolute pathname of a directory where the generated SUE files will be placed. The default is a local subdirectory named "sue".

suppress_progress_messages: Ordinarily the tool will report what cell it is working on, which is reassuring and helpful for debugging, but may obscure important warning messages. This option will suppress progress reports; only warning messages will be displayed.

continue_on_translate_errors: Ordinary the tool will abort with an error message when it encounters a situation it doesn't understand. Specifying this option will cause the tool to continue; obviously results will be unpredictable; a segmentation exception or invalid output may occur.

literal_netnames: Net names syntax is somewhat variable among CAD tools. Ordinarily edif2sue will convert the names into a format acceptable to SUE. Note that this may require generating buscombine psuedo-devices and additional generated names. The generated files may be more readable if the original netnames are presented exactly as they are in EDIF, which this option will do; but note that in this case the generated files may not be netlistable.

ignore_property <property_name>: It may be found that some properties are not useful for SUE and cause excessive clutter; for example, the Cadence port_order property. This option causes all instances of the named property to be ignored. The option should be specified as often as required to ignore multiple properties, such as: 

      ignore_property pin 
      ignore_property schType 
      ignore_property instancesLastChanged 
      ignore_property lastSchematicExtraction 
      
     

use_global <cell_name> <global_name> {<orientation>}: This option says that an instance of <cell_name> should be treated as an instance of the SUE global <global_name>. The optional orientation parameter specifies how the global symbol should be displayed, for example: 

      use_global VDD! vdd RXY

says that a reference to VDD! turns into a SUE global called vdd, and the symbol is displayed "upside down" (above its connection point).

parse_only: Don't translate the file, just parse it and reconstitute the file to stdout. This has been occasionally useful for debugging. It also leads to uniform prettyprinting.

skip_bad_ports: We have discovered some Cadence files that contain duplicate port implementations for some net bundle signals. For example, a cell might have a port called DIN<7:0> (actually a rename of this value), and portimplementations for DIN<3:0>, DIN<7>, and whatever, in addition to a portimplementation for DIN<7:0>. This is quite against the EDIF standard, but what can one do? This hack around just hopes that if the tool can't find a port name that exactly matches the portimplementation reference, it is an instance of this case and can be ignored. Obviously the option should only be invoked if the EDIF file is observed to exhibit this anomaly. If a port is skipped, a warning message is printed.

ignore_property <property_name>: Properties with this name will be silently skipped over wherever encountered. This is for clutter reduction, and also makes it easier to produce netlists usable by SPICE.

use_global <cell_name> <global_name> <orientation>: Rather than create an instance of a cell with this name (such as VSS!), link this net with the MMI global_name (such as gnd). If orientation is specified, apply that transformation to the global symbol, for example, so that vdd symbols will hang down from the top of the schematic as usually expected.

add_verilog_property_by_library <library-name>: Add a Verilog property to cells in the named library, identifying them as base components to the Verilog simulator.

round_to_grid_lines: Snap connection points to the nearest grid lines. WARNING: In some cases this may pull connections apart, resulting in opens.

add_title_bar: This option causes a title bar to be added to each cell.

suppress_instance_name_prefix: This option causes instance names that begin with the specified string to be suppressed; for EDIF files generated from SUE, that prefix is "THING_".

ingore_cell_definition: If a definition for the named cell is encountered, don't create a SUE file for it. If an instance of the cell is encountered in the definition for some other cell, just write it out and hope SUE will know what to do.

scale_coordinates: Multiply all coordinates encountered by the given factor. This might help get a translated schematic on-grid. (Note: in the ordinary course of things, edif2sue will issue a warning if it encounters a coordinate that is off-grid.)

uniquify_duplicate_names: Duplicate names within the same scope are supposed to be illegal in EDIF, but at least one known EDIF writer doesn't respect this for power nets. This option will cause a uniquifying string (__77nn) to be appended to detected duplicate names.

Cadence-Specific Options:

no_skip_bad_ports: In the case of "net splitter" type constructs, the subscripts on a portRef may not match those on the intended corresponding portDef. Strictly speaking this is a violation of the EDIF standard, but since we have enough information to do the right thing, we go ahead an connect the nets as probably intended. If this option is specified, warning messages will be printed when a mismatch is encountered, for human verification if desired.

cadence_property_conversion: Cadence properties sometimes use a macro-substitution language; that is, they are not intended to be treated as the simple strings which they appear to be in the EDIF syntax. If this option is specified, we make a stab at interpreting the property.

show_rippers: A Cadence "ripper" is a pseudo-device with one port that extracts a subset from a bus or net bundle. Since it has only one port, SUE believes that the two sides of the ripper are shorted together, with bad results. Therefore edif2sue normally suppresses the rippers and the wire segments connected to them. SUE matches the nets by name, so the schematic produced is equivalent. If it is desired to view the schematics exactly as they are presented in the EDIF, this option should be invoked. Note that in this case the generated files may not be netlistable.

Parsing

The EDIF file is read in line-by-line. EDIF expressions are converted to a direct internal representation in a recursive top-down fashion; there is very little compaction.

Each expression is read in according to the definitions in the standard. Errors such as missing required fields or illegal fields will be detected and an error message identifying the line number of the error is produced. Name references are resolved as they are encountered in a completely correct manner. Naming errors will generate error messages.

There is no error recovery; a parsing error is immediately fatal.

The process if fairly memory-intensive. Experience shows that the internal representation is about as large as the input file. It is helpful to have that much physical memory available. A large file can take 15-30 minutes to read in.

Extraction

Once parsing has completed successfully, edif2sue will walk over the tree of expressions looking for cell definitions. For each cell definition it will generate a SUE file.

Every effort has been made to make this process robust; that is, to check that the EDIF structure is not just syntactically correct, but is what we expect. In cases where the tool is surprised, as of this writing it will exit with the following message: 

                  fatal error called

This gives an error number and a possibly helpful message. If you see this error message, send a detailed email message along with an example EDIF file to support@micromagic.com.

(One can also specify the "-continue_on_translate_errors" option as a stopgap, but this is obviously dangerous. Parsing errors cannot be continued.)

Some questionable but non-fatal situations will be noted in the standard output, which should be examined carefully when a new design is translated. The option -suppress_progress_messages will make warning messages stand out more clearly.

EDIF Information

The EDIF supported is version 2 0 0 (EIA Recommended Standard EIA-548-1988, dated March 14, 1988). Some information is available from the EDIF Technical Center Web site; see http://edif-tc.cs.man.ac.uk/index.html. Only "level 0" ("the basic level - only literal constants are permitted") is supported; levels 1 and 2 ("addition of parameters and expressions" and "addition of control-flow constructs") are not supported.

As of this writing, edif2sue will not give complete coverage for all legal EDIF constructs; however, meaningful error messages should be produced in cases where the tool becomes confused.

There is also some question about how various CAD tools map their internal databases into EDIF; there is plenty of room for idiosyncrasies or outright incorrectness. The following idiosyncrasies have been seen in the described tools:

Cadence

    • Net "joined" structure is not right for nets with complex names (see Cadence documentation on "iterated names" to understand how they have created a difficult problem for themselves) (for edif2sue, we use the "figure" drawing information to generate the schematics; we are unable to cross-check the figures against the joins in all cases.)
      •

    • "ripper" cells have only one port (EDIF spec specifies that cell-type RIPPER objects have two ports); Cadence has geometrical rules to determine which nets connected to a ripper cell are connected to each other. (edif2sue suppresses the cells and their attached wire segments)
      •

    • Portimplementation references don't always match port definitions for net bundles; see above concerning the "skip_bad_ports" option

    • Indentation is deplorable (the et pretty command will fix it up, if desired)
      •

Synopsys

Limited experience, but no discrepancies have been noted)

Tanner

Duplicate net names for power nets (as, "VddB")

SUE To EDIF Translator: "sue2edif"

sue2edif is a plug-in addition to SUE for writing an EDIF design file based on the current design loaded in SUE. sue2edif requires a special license to execute. This program is used when you want to import SUE schematics into another schematic editor.

Installation

To install the EDIF writer, you need to add the following line to your .suerc file: 

      menu_add -menu file -label "Write EDIF" -command edif_write -position 10 \ 
                             -help "Writes the EDIF for the given schematic and descendents."

Typically, this line is added to the site-wide .suerc file in $MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/sue/.suerc, so that all users can access it. The .suerc file in mmi_local.sample provided with the release includes this line commented out. You need only uncomment it.

When the tool has been properly installed, a new command Write EDIF will appear in the SUE File menu.

Operation

Display the schematic view of the top-level cell of the design file to be written.

Click on the Write EDIF command in the File menu.

SUE will cycle through all included cells in the hierarchy of the current design. Progress messages are displayed on the SUE Message Area and in the SUE command window (the shell window from which you started SUE).

When the command is complete with no errors, the command window displays the message Done. The output EDIF file is written to the same directory as the top cell but with the ".edif" extension.

Output

The EDIF file is a correct representation according to Version 2 0 0, published as "EIA Recommended Standard EIA-548-1988", dated March 14, 1988. Only "level 0" constructs are used.

The file written is an EDIF representation of the design selected. Each SUE cell called for in the design appears as a "cell" definition in the EDIF file. All the cells are organized into a single EDIF library within the file.

Cells are written for all constructs, including library components such as transistors and informational constructs such as title bars, so the complete design as it appears in SUE will be available to be imported into whatever other CAD tool.

The output file will be accurately read by the MMI EDIF conversion tool "edif2sue". The resulting set of SUE files reconstructs the original design. The correct operation of readers for other CAD tools is obviously beyond our control, but we would like to hear about difficulties and are willing to try to "make it work".

A Note on Nets

EDIF contains redundant information describing nets; there is logical connectivity information in "joined" expressions, and there is graphical information in "display" expressions.

SUE uses the graphical information to construct its internal representation of the design, so "what you see is what you get." In other tools this may not be true, and discrepancies between the connectivity and graphical information may cause unpredictable problems.

The generated EDIF file contains correct connectivity information. In some cases a name_net_s component is used in a SUE schematic to select a subset of wires from a bus. EDIF has no way of representing this kind of construction directly, so what the tool does is create separate "joined" statements for each bit of buses which are "split" in this way. These individual nets have names like "bit[3]" and contain a joined statement that lists the one-bit-wide ports connected by this net; there is no graphical information. There is also a net with a name like "bit[7:0]" which contains the graphical information for all bits of the net, but no explicit connectivity information. The name_net_sâ€™s appear as distinct instances in the ordinary way.

If there is a problem with importing the generated EDIF file into other CAD tools, this is likely where it will be, due to the basic incompatibility of the various representations.
